items.title: Your custom logic grid
items.question:
This is an invented logic grid. Each position contains exactly one value from each group, and each value is used once. Positions run from 1 to 3, left to right. Values in the same position are paired.
Animal: Tiger, Lion, Owl.
Colour: Red, Blue, Green.
Drink: Tea, Coffee, Milk.
Clues:
1. Tiger is before Lion.
2. Owl cannot be next to Tiger.
3. Tiger is paired with Red.
4. Blue is paired with Coffee.
5. Tea is in position 1.
6. Lion is paired with Milk.
Which value from Drink is paired with Lion?
items.correctExplanation: The unique complete arrangement gives Milk. Every stated rule holds.
items.incorrectExplanation: Check the clue combinations. The unique complete arrangement gives Milk. Every stated rule holds.
items.lessonContent:
Place each group value exactly once.
Translate each clue into positions or pairings.
Combine clues across groups to eliminate impossible arrangements.
Check all clues against the completed table.
Share this: explain which combination of clues fixed the answer.

items.title: Discover a number rule
items.question:
Topic labels used for this invented example: REEF, SALT, METEOR, CRATER, WHALE.
A display follows this rule: multiply by 6 each time. It shows 17, 102, 612, 3672, 22032, 132192. What value comes next?
items.correctExplanation: The next operation is to multiply by 6. Apply it to 132192 to get 793152.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 793152. The next operation is to multiply by 6. Apply it to 132192 to get 793152.
items.lessonContent:
Look for the rule shared by every example.
Test the rule on the next case, rather than guessing from one example.
Reject a rule that fails any stated example.
Check the answer with exact arithmetic or finite enumeration.
Share this: explain which example gave the decisive clue.

items.title: Space, Ocean · Find the impossible clue
items.question:
Topic labels: space, ocean.
Arrange these cards once each from left to right: REEF, SALT, METEOR, CRATER, WHALE.
Base clues:
REEF is somewhere to the left of METEOR.
CRATER is somewhere to the left of REEF.
METEOR is somewhere to the left of WHALE.
SALT is somewhere to the left of CRATER.
Test these statements:
Statement A: SALT is somewhere to the left of CRATER.
Statement B: METEOR is somewhere to the left of WHALE.
Statement C: WHALE is somewhere to the left of CRATER.
Statement D: REEF is somewhere to the left of METEOR.
Which statement is impossible together with the base clues? Answer A, B, C or D.
items.correctExplanation: Statement C contradicts the order forced by the base clues. The other three statements are compatible.
items.incorrectExplanation: Statement C contradicts the order forced by the base clues. The other three statements are compatible.
items.lessonContent:
Connect the stated before-relations into a chain.
Check each candidate statement against the forced order.
One statement must fail while the others remain possible.
Use the contradiction, not a real-world fact about a label.
Share this: identify the chain that made the impossible clue fail.

proofs.scope: only the stated fictional ordering clues
steps: The base clues force the order SALT, CRATER, REEF, METEOR, WHALE.
The impossible statement reverses a chain of 3 before-relations.
Every other statement agrees with that order.

items.title: Space, Ocean · Plan the best next question
items.question:
Topic: space, ocean. This is an invented card puzzle; the labels do not imply real-world properties.
A hidden card must be identified exactly. The prior probabilities are:
MOON: 4/20, TELESCOPE: 2/20, CORAL: 4/20, CRATER: 4/20, SALT: 6/20.
You can ask only the four yes/no questions below. Every answer is truthful; each question costs one unit. You can adapt later questions to earlier answers, and stop only when one card remains possible.
Question A: Is the hidden card in {MOON}?
Question B: Is the hidden card in {TELESCOPE}?
Question C: Is the hidden card in {CRATER}?
Question D: Is the hidden card in {TELESCOPE, CORAL, CRATER}?
Which FIRST question minimizes the expected TOTAL number of questions, including itself, if all subsequent choices are optimal?
items.correctExplanation: Question D is uniquely optimal: its expected total is 23/10 questions. The planner checks both branches recursively until exact identification.
items.incorrectExplanation: Recheck the stated assumptions. Question D is uniquely optimal: its expected total is 23/10 questions. The planner checks both branches recursively until exact identification.
items.lessonContent:
Represent the possible states and the rules explicitly before choosing an answer.
For deduction, eliminate arrangements that violate even one clue.
For probability, combine prior weights with the stated evidence model.
For planning, consider both possible answers and the questions needed afterwards.
Share this: explain why the closest alternative fails or costs more.

steps: Start with Question A: optimal expected total 13/5 questions.
Start with Question B: optimal expected total 14/5 questions.
Start with Question C: optimal expected total 13/5 questions.
Start with Question D: optimal expected total 23/10 questions.
If the card is MOON: D=no → A=yes.
If the card is TELESCOPE: D=yes → C=no → B=yes.
If the card is CORAL: D=yes → C=no → B=no.
If the card is CRATER: D=yes → C=yes.
If the card is SALT: D=no → A=no.
proofs.scope: optimal among the four stated, noiseless, unit-cost questions and given priors

items.title: Space, Ocean · Bayesian evidence
items.question:
Topic: space, ocean. This is an invented card puzzle; the labels do not imply real-world properties.
A fictional scanner hides one labelled card. Its prior selection probabilities are proportional to the weights below. Each readout is positive or negative. Readouts are independent CONDITIONAL ON the hidden card; a negative readout has probability 1 minus the listed positive probability.
KELP: prior weight 1; P(readout 1 positive | KELP) = 6/10; P(readout 2 positive | KELP) = 9/10
WHALE: prior weight 6; P(readout 1 positive | WHALE) = 5/10; P(readout 2 positive | WHALE) = 8/10
ECLIPSE: prior weight 2; P(readout 1 positive | ECLIPSE) = 4/10; P(readout 2 positive | ECLIPSE) = 6/10
PLANET: prior weight 7; P(readout 1 positive | PLANET) = 7/10; P(readout 2 positive | PLANET) = 4/10
Observed: readout 1 positive, readout 2 positive. Which hidden card is now MOST LIKELY?
items.correctExplanation: WHALE has the largest posterior probability, 120/269. Multiply each prior weight by its observed-readout likelihoods, then divide by the sum of all four products. Most likely is not certain.
items.incorrectExplanation: Recheck the stated assumptions. WHALE has the largest posterior probability, 120/269. Multiply each prior weight by its observed-readout likelihoods, then divide by the sum of all four products. Most likely is not certain.
items.lessonContent:
Represent the possible states and the rules explicitly before choosing an answer.
For deduction, eliminate arrangements that violate even one clue.
For probability, combine prior weights with the stated evidence model.
For planning, consider both possible answers and the questions needed afterwards.
Share this: explain why the closest alternative fails or costs more.

steps: KELP: prior weight 1 × 3/5 × 9/10; normalized posterior 27/269.
WHALE: prior weight 6 × 1/2 × 4/5; normalized posterior 120/269.
ECLIPSE: prior weight 2 × 2/5 × 3/5; normalized posterior 24/269.
PLANET: prior weight 7 × 7/10 × 2/5; normalized posterior 98/269.
WHALE has the largest posterior. This means most likely under the model, not certain.
proofs.scope: the explicitly stated priors, fictional readouts and conditional independence
